statement: A factory's cost, in thousands of dollars, to remove $p$ percent of a pollutant from its wastewater is modeled by $C(p) = \dfrac{120p}{100 - p}$ for $0 \le p < 100$. According to the model, how many thousand dollars more does it cost to remove $90\%$ of the pollutant than to remove $80\%$ of it?

choices.misconception: I subtracted the percents first and computed $C(10) = \frac{1{,}200}{90} \approx 13$, but $C(90) - C(80)$ is not the same as $C(90 - 80)$.

I found $C(80) = 480$, which is $6$ per percent, and assumed every extra percent costs the same $6$, so $10$ more percent costs $60$. The denominator shrinks as $p$ nears $100$, so the cost climbs faster and faster.
I computed $C(90) = 1{,}080$, the whole cost of removing $90\%$, but forgot to subtract the cost of removing $80\%$.

hints: Find the cost at each of the two percents, then compare them.

solutions.reliable: Evaluate the model at both percents: $C(90) = \dfrac{120 \cdot 90}{100 - 90} = \dfrac{10{,}800}{10} = 1{,}080$ and $C(80) = \dfrac{120 \cdot 80}{100 - 80} = \dfrac{9{,}600}{20} = 480$. The difference is $1{,}080 - 480 = 600$ thousand dollars.
solutions.elegant: The graph of $C$ has a vertical asymptote at $p = 100$, which is why the last few percent are so expensive. Going from $80\%$ to $90\%$ cuts the denominator in half, from $20$ to $10$, while the numerator grows, so the cost more than doubles, from $480$ to $1{,}080$. The extra cost is $1{,}080 - 480 = 600$ thousand dollars.
